departure.name: Departures from tradition
departure.description: Words where this translation uses a different English word from the traditional one, with the reason and the standard view.

loanword.name: Names and titles left in Greek
loanword.description: Terms left untranslated because they work as a name or title and every English candidate would mislead.

terms.brief: The personal, pre-existent Word (John 1:1, 1:14; Revelation 19:13; 1 John 1:1).
terms.context:
Kept as a loanword under the three-part test: it is a title, it occurs in four verses, and the English candidate actively misleads. In current usage 'the Word' commonly means the Bible, so 'the Word was God' gives many readers a false meaning, and 'word' alone conveys nothing of what a Greek-speaking reader heard (reason, the ordering principle of the world) or of God's creating speech in Genesis 1. A note is required at John 1:1 covering both backgrounds.

**The standard view.** Nearly all translations use 'Word'. Most scholars see John's main background as the Hebrew Bible's 'word of the Lord' and Wisdom traditions, which 'Word' reflects and 'Logos' does not; the note must say so.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: Gentle, humble, not self-assertive.
terms.context:
'Meek' now suggests weakness, which the Greek does not. 'Gentle' is accurate and plain. Matthew 5:5 echoes Psalm 37:11 (Septuagint 36:11), where the word renders the Hebrew for the humble poor.

**The standard view.** That illustration is widespread in sermons, but I do not know of lexical evidence that it defines the word; it needs checking before it is used. 'Gentle' or 'humble' is the mainstream modern rendering.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: The gathered community of believers, local or as a whole.
terms.context:
A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled. 'Church' now means a building or an institution. One English word everywhere shows the reader it is one Greek word.

**The standard view.** 'Church' is near-universal and readers know what it refers to. 'Assembly' can sound like a one-off meeting.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: To turn around in mind and conduct, toward God.
terms.context:
'Repent' now centres on feeling sorry. In the Gospels the word carries the prophets' call to 'return' to God, a change of direction. 'Change your mind' is too thin and too mental.

**The standard view.** Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term that readers understand as including a change of life.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: The Valley of Hinnom as the place of final judgment.
terms.context:
It is a place name. 'Hell' merges it with Hades and with later imagery. Several modern translations keep the name.

**The standard view.** Many translations still use 'hell', usually with a footnote giving Gehenna.

terms.brief: A person owned by another.
terms.context:
The word meant a slave, and hearers knew it. 'Servant' softens it and blurs the difference from διάκονος and παῖς.

**The standard view.** Several modern translations now use 'slave'; others keep 'servant' or 'bondservant' to avoid association with race-based chattel slavery.

terms.brief: The announcement of good news.
terms.context:
'Gospel' is now a religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, also used of imperial proclamations.

**The standard view.** Many modern translations already alternate between 'good news' and 'gospel'.

terms.brief: Single, sound; in the 'good eye' idiom, generous (Matthew 6:22; Luke 11:34).
terms.context:
In Matthew the saying sits between treasure in heaven and serving Mammon, and the 'evil eye' that follows is a known Jewish idiom for stinginess, so 'generous' fits the context.

**The standard view.** Most translations use 'healthy' or 'sound', keeping the physical image of the eye, and mention generosity in a footnote. The physical image is lost with 'generous'.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: Only one of its kind; an only child.
terms.context:
The second half of the word comes from 'kind', not 'beget'. 'One and only' is the mainstream modern rendering.

**The standard view.** A minority of scholars have recently defended 'only begotten'.

terms.brief: The cover of the ark where atonement was made; a means of atonement.
terms.context:
In the Septuagint the word is the name of the ark's cover, which is how Hebrews 9:5 uses it; using the same phrase in Romans 3:25 lets the reader see the allusion.

**The standard view.** Whether Romans 3:25 means 'mercy seat', 'propitiation' (turning away wrath) or 'expiation' (removing sin) is a long-running dispute.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: One called alongside to help, especially an advocate.
terms.context:
Outside the New Testament the word is used of someone who speaks on another's behalf, and 1 John 2:1 clearly uses it that way. The loanword 'Paraclete' is not used.

**The standard view.** 'Advocate', 'Helper' and 'Counselor' are all in current use.

terms.brief: Sexual relations outside what the law permits.
terms.context:
A broad term; 'fornication' is obsolete and narrower.

**The standard view.** Same as the default.

terms.brief: To have received in full (the wording of a receipt), in Matthew 6:2, 6:5, 6:16 and Luke 6:24.
terms.context:
The verb is the standard term on surviving receipts from the period, so hearers would have caught the commercial tone.

**The standard view.** Modern translations commonly render 'have received their reward in full'.

terms.brief: Sibling; in the plural, fellow members of the community.
terms.context:
In Greek the masculine plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of siblings, so the first hearers in a mixed assembly understood the women to be included. English 'brothers' now reads as men only.

**The standard view.** Several modern translations use 'brothers and sisters'; more formal ones keep 'brothers' with a footnote saying the word can include women.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: Used as a noun in the plural for the members of the community (οἱ ἅγιοι).
terms.context:
'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel.

**The standard view.** Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people' or 'his holy people'.

terms.brief: To transfer a person or thing into another's custody, power or control.
terms.context:
The verb is the ordinary Greek word for handing a person or thing into someone else's control. The Gospels use the same word for what Judas does, what the priests do to Jesus before Pilate, what Pilate does, and what will happen to the disciples. Greek has a separate word for betrayal, used of Judas in Luke 6:16. "Betray" names the treachery that the context supplies, but it hides that chain of handings-over, so one rendering lets the reader see what the Greek reader saw. The self-giving formulas keep the familiar "give up" because "hand himself over for me" is awkward English and adds no clarity.

**The standard view.** Most English versions (KJV, RSV, ESV, NIV, NRSV) render "betray" when Judas is the subject and "deliver", "hand over" or "give up" elsewhere. They usually say "arrested" or "put in prison" for John in Matt 4:12 and Mark 1:14, and "gave up his spirit" in John 19:30. The standard lexicons give "hand over, deliver up" as the basic sense. Many scholars hold that "betray" is a contextual inference and not the word's meaning, while others defend it as a legitimate contextual sense for Judas. The NABRE and several recent commentators use "hand over" more widely, as here.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: A deed that displays supernatural power, a miracle.
terms.context:
The Greek word is simply the ordinary word for power used of a concrete act, and a first-century reader would have heard that connection. "Deed of power" keeps the connection visible where the same word appears nearby as "power" (Mark 6:2 with 6:14; Acts 8:10 with 8:13; 1 Cor 12), which "miracle" hides. It also keeps the word distinct from "sign" and "wonder" in the triads at Acts 2:22, 2 Cor 12:12 and Heb 2:4.

**The standard view.** There is no dispute about the meaning, only about the English. The KJV alternates "mighty works" and "miracles"; RSV and ESV favor "mighty works" in the Gospels and "miracles" in the letters; NIV and many others use "miracles" throughout; NRSV largely uses "deeds of power". Standard lexica gloss this sense as deed of power, miracle, or wonder. "Miracle" is a fully acceptable rendering, and the default here is a choice for consistency and transparency, not a correction.

terms.brief: To continue in a place, state or relationship and not leave or cease; includes the Johannine use of persons, God, word or love remaining in someone or something.
terms.context:
The Greek verb is the everyday word for staying or remaining, with no special religious tone. "Abide" is now archaic and carries a devotional colouring the Greek lacks. "Remain" also works for both people and things, so the reader can hear John's deliberate repetition of one verb, for example the branch remaining in the vine, words remaining in the disciples, and fruit that remains.

**The standard view.** KJV, ESV and NRSV keep "abide" in John 15 and 1 John. NIV, CSB, NET and NAB use "remain", and some use "live in" or "continue in" in places. Lexicons gloss the verb as remain, stay, continue, and transitively as await. For lodging, all modern versions use "stay". For permanence, "endure", "last" and "remain" are all common, with "endures forever" usual in the Old Testament quotations.

terms.brief: Pressure in the figurative sense: hardship, oppression or trouble that bears down on a person or people, usually from outside circumstances or hostile parties.
terms.context:
In the period, including the Septuagint, θλῖψις was an ordinary word for oppressive hardship, not a technical term. 'Tribulation' is now heard by many readers as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the Greek does. 'Affliction' is an established traditional rendering alongside it (the King James Version uses both) and carries the idea of hardship pressing on someone. Using it in the Gospels, Paul and Revelation alike lets the reader see the same word in 'great affliction' at Matthew 24:21, Acts 7:11 and Revelation 7:14, and it leaves 'distress' free for στενοχωρία and ἀνάγκη when they are paired with it.

**The standard view.** Lexicons agree on the sense: oppression, affliction, distress, with an occasional inward sense of anguish. English versions split. KJV and ESV alternate between 'tribulation' and 'affliction'; NRSV often has 'suffering', 'affliction', 'distress' or 'ordeal'; NIV uses 'trouble', 'distress', 'suffering', 'hardships' and 'persecution' (Acts 11:19), keeping 'tribulation' only at Revelation 7:14. Many versions retain 'great tribulation' in Matthew 24:21 and Revelation 7:14. Whether Revelation 7:14 refers to a single final crisis or to the whole course of the church's suffering is debated, but that is a question of reference, not of the word's meaning.

terms.brief: The sanctuary building proper, the dwelling place of the God of Israel, as distinct from the whole temple complex with its courts (ἱερόν); this includes the Jerusalem sanctuary, its heavenly counterpart in Revelation, and figurative uses for Jesus' body, the believer's body and the community.
terms.context:
Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both render 'temple': ἱερόν for the whole complex with its courts, and ναός for the building where the deity dwells. Using 'temple' for both blurs passages where the difference matters: Zechariah enters the ναός while the people wait outside, a murder happens between the ναός and the altar, and the outer court lies outside the ναός that is measured. 'Sanctuary' is an accepted rendering used by some mainstream versions. Applying it uniformly, including to the figurative uses, keeps linked sayings such as the destroy-and-rebuild charge and the torn curtain identical across the Gospels, and keeps Paul's image focused on the place where God dwells.

**The standard view.** Most English versions (KJV, ESV, NIV, NASB) render ναός as 'temple' throughout and do not distinguish it from ἱερόν. The NRSV uses 'sanctuary' in some places (for example Matthew 23 and Luke 1) but 'temple' elsewhere, and the HCSB used 'sanctuary' widely. Standard lexicons gloss the word as 'temple' while noting that it refers particularly to the sanctuary building or inner shrine. Scholars differ on how strictly New Testament writers observe the distinction; Matthew 27:5 and John 2:20 are often cited as looser uses. 'You are God's temple' in Paul is deeply established in English.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: To speak defamatory or demeaning words about people, their conduct, or things such as a message, a teaching or angelic beings; the non-divine sense of the verb.
terms.context:
In first-century Greek this verb meant abusive or defamatory speech against anyone, not only against God. Modern English "blaspheme" is confined to irreverence toward God or the sacred, so it misleads when the target is a person, a practice or a teaching. "Slander" is a standard dictionary gloss for those cases. "Blaspheme" is kept where God or the divine is the target, and "insult" serves for jeering to someone's face, where "slander" would wrongly suggest a false report to third parties.

**The standard view.** The lexicons distinguish speech against humans (slander, revile, defame) from speech against God or transcendent beings (blaspheme, speak irreverently of). The KJV uses "blaspheme" widely, alongside "revile", "rail on" and "speak evil of". Modern versions such as the ESV, NRSV and NIV keep "blaspheme" for God-directed uses and vary among revile, slander, malign, insult and heap abuse elsewhere. They differ on boundary cases: several keep "blaspheme" for the word of God, the way of truth or the glorious ones (Titus 2:5, 2 Peter 2:2, 2 Peter 2:10, Jude 8), where this translation uses "slander". In Acts 13:45 and 18:6 some read blasphemy against Christ rather than abuse of Paul.

terms.brief: To put a person or God to the test, whether to prove character, to trap, or by pressure that could make someone fail.
terms.context:
The Greek verb means to put to the test. In the Greek Old Testament it is the ordinary word for God testing Israel and Israel testing God, and Jesus' forty days and the argument of Hebrews both draw on that background. Modern English 'tempt' has narrowed to 'entice to sin', which hides this link and sits badly with suffering and persecution contexts, so 'test' is the default. 'Tempt' is kept where enticement to sin is plainly the point, and 'the tempter' is kept as the title because 'the tester' is not natural English for the devil.

**The standard view.** Most translations use 'tempt' for the devil's approach to Jesus, for Hebrews 2:18 and 4:15, 1 Corinthians 10:13 and James 1:13-14, and 'test' for the Pharisees' questions, the testing of God, Abraham, and Revelation. Some recent versions and many commentators prefer 'test' in the wilderness narratives and in Hebrews. Standard lexicons recognize both 'test' and 'tempt' as contextual senses of the one verb, and it is disputed which fits the wilderness narrative and Hebrews 4:15 ('yet without sin'). 'The tempter' is the near-universal rendering of the title.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: Service rendered or an assigned task carried out on behalf of another, including apostolic and congregational work and the collection for Jerusalem.
terms.context:
In the first century this was an everyday word for service or for carrying out a task for someone, from waiting at table to delivering a commission. It did not denote a religious office. "Ministry" now suggests clergy or a church profession, and it hides the link with the related words rendered "servant" and "serve". "Service" is a recognized lexical gloss, and it works in every context where the word occurs, including Paul's apostolic task and the collection for Jerusalem.

**The standard view.** Most English translations use "ministry" for apostolic and church work, and vary by context elsewhere: "service", "serving" or "preparations" in Luke 10:40, "distribution" in Acts 6:1, "relief" in Acts 11:29, and "mission" or "service" in Acts 12:25 and for the collection. Standard lexicons list service, aid, and office or ministry as glosses. Some scholarship stresses the idea of commissioned agency over humble service; "service" is compatible with either view.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: Assurance and freedom from fear before God or at judgment, including approach to him in prayer or worship (Hebrews, 1 John, 1 Timothy 3:13).
terms.context:
In ordinary Greek the word meant freedom to speak one's mind, and by this period it also meant the assurance of someone who can stand before a superior without fear or shame. For that sense "confidence" is the more accurate modern word, because "boldness" can suggest nerve or audacity, which is not the point when approaching God or facing judgment. "Boldness" is kept where the context is courageous public speech, and "plainly" and "openly" where the word describes the manner of speaking or acting.

**The standard view.** The standard lexicons distinguish plainness or frankness of speech, openness to public view, and courage or confidence, the last especially before God or persons of high rank. The KJV mostly has "boldness" or "boldly" in Acts and the letters; modern versions such as the ESV and NIV largely use "confidence" in Hebrews and 1 John and "boldness" for the preaching in Acts, while the NRSV keeps "boldness" in some of the approach-to-God passages, such as Hebrews 4:16. The choice between the two is a matter of English nuance and not a real dispute about meaning.

terms.brief: Holding out under hardship, opposition or delay; steadfast staying power.
terms.context:
In period usage, including the Septuagint, the word means active staying power under pressure: standing one's ground, not giving up. Modern English "patience" suggests calm waiting or an even temper, which misleads; James 5:11 shows the problem, since Job protests loudly yet holds out. "Endurance" conveys the sense, keeps the word distinct from μακροθυμία (rendered "patience", and paired with it in Colossians 1:11 and 2 Timothy 3:10), and matches the verb ὑπομένω, "endure".

**The standard view.** The KJV has "patience" almost throughout. Modern versions abandon it but divide: NRSV and CSB mostly use "endurance", NIV and NASB often "perseverance", ESV often "steadfastness", and some use "patient endurance" in Revelation. The standard lexicons gloss it as endurance, perseverance, fortitude or steadfastness, so the default is within the mainstream.

terms.brief: To trip someone up, bringing about their fall in faith or loyalty to God, whether into sin, desertion or rejection; in the passive, to be so tripped up.
terms.context:
The verb comes from the Septuagint's word for a trap or obstacle and means to bring about someone's fall in loyalty to God. "Offend" now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak, and "cause to sin" is narrower than the Greek. "Cause to stumble" keeps the picture and the breadth. In the passive, "fall away" is the clearest English where desertion is meant, and "take offense" remains accurate where people are affronted by Jesus or his words.

**The standard view.** The KJV has "offend" throughout. Modern versions divide the active between "cause to sin" (ESV, older NIV) and "cause to stumble" (NASB, NIV 2011, NRSV in places). For the passive they commonly use "fall away" for desertion and "take offense" for Nazareth and the Pharisees. Matt 11:6 is split between "take offense at me" and "stumble on account of me", and John 6:61 between "offend" and "cause to stumble". Standard lexicons distinguish causing a fall or sin, with its passive of falling away or being repelled by someone, from the weaker sense of shocking or giving offense.

terms.brief: A secret, especially a purpose or plan of God kept hidden and now disclosed by him.
terms.context:
In Jewish Greek of the period, notably the Greek Daniel and books such as Tobit and Sirach, this word is the ordinary term for a secret, often God's secret plan that only he can disclose. English 'mystery' now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas the New Testament writers usually stress that the thing has been made known and can be stated plainly. 'Secret' conveys that without the misleading overtone. In 1 Cor 2:7 the phrase may be recast with 'secret' as a modifier, for example 'God's secret wisdom'.

**The standard view.** Most English versions (KJV, ESV, NASB, NIV 2011) keep 'mystery' throughout, treating it as an established technical term and explaining it as a truth once hidden and now revealed. Many scholars defend that practice. Some versions use 'secret' in places: RSV, NRSV and NIV have 'secret' or 'secrets' in the Gospel sayings, and NIV has 'secret power' at 2 Thess 2:7. Lexicons give 'secret' as a primary gloss, so the default is lexically sound, but it is an editorial choice against the majority tradition.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.traditional: abolish, make void, destroy, do away
terms.brief: To deprive something of force or effect, put it out of operation or bring it to an end; the default governs cases where the object is a law, promise, covenant commitment or the like whose validity is at stake.
terms.context:
In the usage of the period, and above all in Paul, this verb means to make something idle or inoperative: to take away its force, or to bring it to an end. It is not the ordinary word for destroying, and it does not mean to fade. English has no single word that fits a law, a promise, death, hostile rulers and childish ways alike, so this translation fixes one rendering for each kind of object. 'Nullify' is the default for laws and promises, where the question is whether they still hold.

**The standard view.** The standard lexicons give the senses as: use up or waste (Luke 13:7); make ineffective or nullify; abolish, set aside or bring to an end; and, in the passive with 'from', be released or estranged. Mainstream translations vary the English freely, with 'nullify', 'make void', 'abolish', 'destroy', 'bring to nothing', 'pass away', 'release' and 'sever' all in use. Many have 'destroy' at 1 Corinthians 15:24-26 and Hebrews 2:14. Several have 'fading' for the glory in 2 Corinthians 3; some scholars defend that as a contextual sense, but others reject it as lacking lexical support. Romans 6:6 is divided between 'destroyed', 'done away with' and 'rendered powerless'.

terms.brief: To make holy: to bring a person or thing into the sphere of what belongs to God, whether by cultic contact, by Christ's offering, or by the Spirit.
terms.context:
The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for 'holy', and a first-century reader would have heard that link every time. 'Make holy' keeps it visible, for example in 1 Corinthians 7:14 and Hebrews 2:11, where 'sanctify' hides it. 'Sanctify' also now suggests to many readers a technical doctrine of gradual moral improvement, which is not the point in most occurrences. Where the object is already holy (God's name, Christ) or is being dedicated to a task, 'make holy' would mislead, so the alternates apply.

**The standard view.** Most mainstream translations (KJV, ESV, NRSV, NASB) use 'sanctify' for most occurrences and 'hallowed' in the Lord's Prayer. Several (NIV, NLT, NJB and others) use 'make holy' in many places, and 'consecrate' or 'set apart' in John 10:36 and 17:17-19. The standard lexicons gloss the verb as 'make holy, consecrate, sanctify' and, with God or his name as object, 'treat as holy, reverence'. The meaning itself is not in dispute; the choice among these English words is one of register and clarity.

terms.brief: To win a victory over an opponent or hostile power; to be the victor (used with an object or absolutely).
terms.context:
The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning in battle, in the games or in court, and is cognate with the noun for 'victory'. 'Conquer' keeps that note of victory. 'Overcome' in modern English tends to suggest merely getting past a difficulty, and it hides the link between Jesus' victory in John 16:33, the believers' victory in 1 John, and the victor promises in Revelation.

**The standard view.** The KJV uses 'overcome' almost everywhere, and the NIV and NASB largely keep it. The ESV and NRSV use 'conquer' in Revelation, and the NRSV also in John 16:33 and 1 John, though both keep 'overcome' in Romans 12:21; in 1 John the ESV keeps 'overcome'. Lexica give 'be victor, conquer, overcome, prevail', and agree that Romans 3:4 is the legal sense of winning a case. The meaning is not in dispute; the choice between 'conquer' and 'overcome' is one of English register and consistency.

terms.brief: Tent: a portable or temporary structure, including Israel's wilderness tent-sanctuary and its heavenly counterpart.
terms.context:
The Greek word is the ordinary one for a tent, and the Greek Old Testament uses the same plain word for Israel's portable sanctuary and for the huts of the Feast of Booths. 'Tabernacle' is a Latin-derived word that now sounds like a special religious object and hides the plain image, while 'tent' lets the reader hear what a first-century reader heard. Using 'tent' in all three transfiguration accounts, and in Luke 16:9 and Acts 15:16, keeps the parallels aligned and the Old Testament echoes audible.

**The standard view.** Older versions (KJV, NASB) use 'tabernacle' for the sanctuary and often for the transfiguration. ESV and NRSV use 'tent' widely, including in Hebrews, while NIV keeps 'tabernacle' for the sanctuary and uses 'shelters' at the transfiguration. For Luke 16:9 most modern versions generalise to 'dwellings' or 'homes'. In Revelation 21:3 versions divide among 'tabernacle', 'dwelling' and 'home'. Lexicons agree the word means tent, hut or temporary lodging, and by extension a dwelling.

terms.brief: A putting to the proof: an experience or ordeal that tests a person's faithfulness; less often, enticement to do wrong.
terms.context:
In the usage of the period, including the Greek Old Testament, this word mainly means a putting to the proof, an experience that shows whether someone will stay faithful. English 'temptation' has narrowed to enticement to sin, so in most passages it now misleads; in the Lord's Prayer, for instance, it suggests God might lure people into wrongdoing. 'Testing' keeps the link with the related verb 'to test', while 'trial' is kept for hardships endured and 'temptation' for the one passage about enticement by desire.

**The standard view.** Most English versions keep 'temptation' in the Lord's Prayer, the Gethsemane sayings, 1 Cor 10:13 and 1 Tim 6:9, and use 'trial' or 'testing' in Luke 8:13, Acts 20:19, Hebrews, James, 1 and 2 Peter and Rev 3:10. Some, such as the NRSV, have 'time of trial' in the Lord's Prayer and Gethsemane. Lexicons recognize both senses, test or trial and enticement to sin, and scholars disagree on which is in view in the Lord's Prayer and in 1 Cor 10:13, where the two overlap, so the default there is an editorial choice and should carry a note.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: A wrongful act, a violation of what is right, committed against God or another person.
terms.context:
In this period the word means a wrong or moral failure, and an act of wrongdoing is what a first-century reader would have heard in it. 'Trespass' in current English chiefly suggests entering property without permission, so it now misleads more than 'offense', which standard lexicons give as a gloss and which the King James Version itself uses in Romans 5. 'Offense' also keeps the word distinct from 'sin' (ἁμαρτία) and 'transgression' (παράβασις), which stand beside it in Romans 5 and Ephesians 2:1.

**The standard view.** The meaning is not disputed, but English versions differ on the word. The Tyndale and KJV tradition, the ESV and the NRSV mostly have 'trespass'; the NASB and NET favor 'transgression'; the NIV often has 'sin' and keeps 'trespass' in Romans 5; the KJV in Romans 5 and the CSB in several places have 'offense'. In Romans 11:11-12 versions vary between 'trespass', 'transgression' and 'stumbling'.

terms.brief: One who robs with violence, typically armed and often in a gang; a brigand or highwayman, as distinct from a thief who steals by stealth.
terms.context:
Greek distinguishes this word from the one for a thief who steals by stealth; this one denotes an armed, violent plunderer such as a highwayman or brigand. 'Robber' is not wrong, but in modern English it can suggest a burglar or mugger, and the KJV's 'thief' blurs the distinction altogether. 'Bandit' keeps the element of violence and outlawry, fits every New Testament occurrence, and leaves room for the insurgent overtone some see in the Passion narratives without asserting it. A single rendering also keeps the word recognisably the same across the temple saying, the arrest, the crucifixion and Barabbas.

**The standard view.** Standard lexicons gloss the word as robber, highwayman or bandit, and note that it was also applied to insurrectionists, as in Josephus. Most modern translations (ESV, NASB, NIV in most places) use 'robber'; the NRSV uses 'bandit' in many of these verses. Some versions render it 'rebel', 'revolutionary' or 'insurrectionist' for the men crucified with Jesus, at the arrest scene, or for Barabbas; that reading is possible but not certain. The KJV's 'thieves' in the temple saying and the crucifixion is generally regarded as imprecise.

terms.brief: To slaughter: to butcher an animal, especially for sacrifice, and by extension to kill a person violently and bloodily.
terms.context:
The Greek verb is the ordinary word for butchering an animal, used in the Septuagint for sacrificial slaughter and also for brutal killing of people; it is not the common word for 'kill'. 'Slain' is now archaic and solemn and loses that bluntness, while 'kill' or 'murder' loses the butchery image that ties the Lamb, the martyrs and Cain's victim together. Using 'slaughter' everywhere, including Revelation 13:3, also lets the reader see that the beast's wounded head is described with the same word as the Lamb.

**The standard view.** Standard lexicons gloss the verb as 'slaughter', and also 'murder' for violent killing of persons. Most English versions use 'slain' for the Lamb and the martyrs in Revelation, though some modern versions use 'slaughtered' there. In 1 John 3:12 most have 'murdered', 'killed' or 'slew'. In Revelation 13:3 most paraphrase as 'a mortal wound', 'wounded to death' or 'fatal wound' rather than keeping the verb.

terms.brief: A specialist in interpreting the Jewish Law (the Gospel occurrences).
terms.context:
In the Gospels the word names men learned in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, a group overlapping with those called scribes. To a modern reader 'lawyer' suggests an attorney representing clients in court, which misleads. 'Expert in the law' says what a first-century reader would have understood. The lowercase 'law' is fixed here only for consistency within the phrase.

**The standard view.** Lexicons gloss the noun as one learned in the law, a legal expert, and in the Gospels specifically an expert in the Mosaic law. The KJV, RSV, NRSV, ESV and NASB keep 'lawyer'. The NIV, NET and CSB use 'expert in the law' or something close to it. For Zenas in Titus 3:13 nearly all versions have 'lawyer', and commentators are divided on whether he was a Roman jurist or a Jewish legal expert.

terms.brief: Person afflicted with the ritually defiling scaly skin condition of Leviticus 13-14 (the only sense in the New Testament).
terms.context:
In the Septuagint and in first-century Jewish usage this word names someone with the condition regulated in Leviticus 13-14: a range of scaly skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean, which is why they are 'cleansed' and not simply healed. 'Leper' and 'leprosy' today mean Hansen's disease, which is narrower than the Greek term and may not even be included in it, so the traditional word misleads a modern reader about what is described. 'Skin disease' is the description standard lexicons give. The familiar byname of Simon is kept because it identifies him rather than diagnoses him.

**The standard view.** Most major translations (KJV, ESV, NRSV, NET) keep 'leper', and NIV and CSB use 'person with leprosy', usually with a footnote saying the term covers various skin diseases. A minority, such as the CEB and the HCSB ('serious skin disease'), put that in the text. Scholars widely agree the biblical term is broader than modern leprosy. The disagreement is whether to keep the familiar word with a note, since 'skin disease' can understate the severity and social exclusion involved.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: A course of action one has committed to, such as a plan, project or firm stand.
terms.context:
In the usage of the period the word normally refers to something objective: what underlies or stands firm, an underlying reality, or a plan or project one has taken on. Lexicographers have questioned whether the inner feeling 'confidence' is securely attested for it. 'Undertaking' suits Paul's collection project and his project of boasting. At Hebrews 3:14 the related use for a firm stand gives 'resolve', which fits the call to hold fast. This is an editorial choice in a disputed area, and 'confidence' remains defensible.

**The standard view.** Most English versions (KJV, ESV, NIV and others) render 'confidence', 'confident' or 'conviction' at 2 Corinthians 9:4, 11:17 and Hebrews 3:14. The NRSV has 'undertaking' at 2 Corinthians 9:4 but 'confidence' at the other two. At Hebrews 11:1 most modern versions have 'assurance' or 'confidence' (KJV 'substance'), though some have 'reality', and many commentators favor an objective sense. At Hebrews 1:3 'being' or 'nature' is standard (KJV 'person'). The standard modern lexicon and specialist word studies argue against 'confidence' and for 'plan, undertaking', 'situation' or 'reality'. Scholarship is divided, and the traditional rendering is still widely defended.

Scholars disagree on this word, and this rendering is an editorial choice.

terms.brief: A first payment that secures a transaction and commits the payer to the rest; used figuratively of the Spirit given to believers.
terms.context:
In the commercial Greek of the period the word meant money paid in advance that both forms part of the full payment and binds the payer to complete it. "Earnest" in this sense is no longer understood by modern readers, and "guarantee" or "pledge" conveys the assurance but loses the idea that part of the thing itself has already been handed over. "Down payment" is ordinary modern English that keeps both ideas, and standard lexicons list it among the glosses.

**The standard view.** The KJV has "earnest". Modern versions divide: ESV and NKJV use "guarantee", NASB "pledge", NIV "deposit" with "guaranteeing" added, NRSV "first installment" in 2 Corinthians and "pledge" in Ephesians, and CSB and NET "down payment". Scholars agree it is a commercial loanword from Semitic for earnest money or a deposit; in the Septuagint of Genesis 38 it is a pledge that is later returned, so some prefer "pledge", but the part-payment sense is the common commercial one and fits Paul's use of the Spirit as a first share of what is to come.
